title: Rivers of living water (John 7:25–52)
hookLine: on the great day of the feast he cries: let anyone thirsty come

cards: A golden pitcher, a pool, and a procession at dawn.

According to Jewish tradition written down in the Mishnah, on the mornings of the Feast of Tabernacles a priest walked down to the pool of Siloam, filled a golden pitcher, and carried it back up to the temple, with crowds and music.
At the altar, he poured the water out. In a dry land waiting for the winter rains, that poured-out water meant something. Now it's the last day of the feast, the greatest day.
And in the middle of the crowds, Jesus stands up and shouts.

teach.b: "In the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink."
Then: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water." Belly is the old, literal word.
Here it means the deepest inside of a person, which is why some modern translations say heart.
And there's a puzzle: whose heart? The sentence can be read two ways: rivers flowing out of the believer, or out of Jesus himself, for anyone who comes and drinks. Readers have taken it both ways.
John explains in the next verse: Jesus was speaking about the Spirit, which those who believed would receive. A woman at a well heard about living water. A crowd heard about bread.
Now, at a festival of water, Jesus offers rivers. And the crowd splits. Some say he's the prophet, some the Christ.
Others say the Christ can't come from Galilee. Officers sent to arrest him come back empty-handed. Why didn't you bring him?

teach.h: NEVER MAN SPAKE LIKE THIS MAN.

teach.b: And one quiet voice on the council speaks up: Nicodemus, who came by night in chapter three. Shouldn't we hear a man before judging him? He's beginning to come out of the dark.

how: Christians often read this passage at Pentecost, connecting the rivers of living water with the gift of the Holy Spirit; many also connect it with baptism.

practice: If you have a glass of water near you, hold it; if not, picture one, and think about where it came from: rain, a river, pipes under your street, the people who keep them working.
Take a slow sip and notice that your body needed it, even if you didn't feel thirsty. If you pray, give thanks for the water; if you don't, give thanks for the glass in your hand.
